text: Causes are of three types, distinguished by their mode of relation: inherent, non-inherent, and efficient. That which is inherently present in the effect is the inherent cause; for example, the threads are the inherent cause of the cloth, and the cloth is the inherent cause of its own color and other properties. When the cause is present in the same entity as the effect, either together with the effect or with the cause, it is the non-inherent cause; for example, the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause of the cloth, and the form of the threads is the non-inherent cause of the form of the cloth. A cause distinct from both of these is the efficient cause; for example, the loom and so on are the efficient cause of the cloth. Among these three types of causes, that which is the non-universal cause is precisely the operative cause. || 37 ||
